channel.title: Blockheight
channel.description: Blockheight reports crypto news: Bitcoin and Ethereum, DeFi protocols, exchanges, stablecoins, regulation, security incidents and market structure.

item.title: Why Rebalance a Solana CLMM Position After It Exits?
item.description: A Solana CLMM position outside its price range stops earning swap fees; rebalance only when restoring active liquidity is worth the swap and upkeep costs.

item.title: How TRON Bandwidth and Energy Set Transfer Costs
item.description: TRON uses Bandwidth for transaction data and Energy for smart-contract work; learn when USDT transfers spend each resource and how to check the likely cost.

item.title: Four checks for reading TRON event-log costs
item.description: TRON event logs show what a contract emitted, while receipt fields show Energy use and TRX fees; four checks help separate execution, payer, penalties and bandwidth.

item.title: Why a TRON USDT Transfer Can Cost 6 or 13 TRX
item.description: A TRON USDT transfer can burn about 6 TRX to a funded wallet or 13 TRX to a new token recipient, depending on Energy, address state and resources.

item.title: How to Turn XMR Into Stablecoins Before a Token Buy
item.description: To move XMR toward a token purchase, convert it into a stablecoin accepted on the token’s network, then verify the deposit chain and contract before trading.

item.title: How to size a Monero payout buffer
item.description: Size a Monero payout buffer from the XMR owed before the next refill, then add fees and a margin for demand, settlement time and price movement.

item.title: Selling Tokens After Genesis Liquidity Opens
item.description: Selling after genesis liquidity opens is a sequence of checks: confirm the pool, size the order against depth, then verify the swap and proceeds on-chain.

item.title: Check Swap Pool Contracts Before Treasury Trades
item.description: Treasury teams can verify a swap pool by matching its address, token pair and fee settings to protocol records, then checking the code and trade route.

item.title: Fund an Avalanche Wallet Before You Swap
item.description: A swap on Avalanche’s C-Chain needs AVAX for network fees; fund the wallet by sending compatible assets or bridging them, then confirm the network and token.

item.title: How to Estimate Slippage Before an Avalanche Token Swap
item.description: A swap quote estimates output; slippage tolerance sets the minimum you accept if Avalanche prices move, while price impact reflects trade size against pool liquidity.

item.title: Base withdrawals still tie up exit liquidity for five days
item.description: Base’s five-day canonical withdrawal window still ties up capital; how bridge delays shape exits, liquidity planning and faster routes traders may use.

item.title: How to Set a Slippage Limit for Wallet Swaps
item.description: A slippage limit caps how far a wallet swap can move from its quote; set the lowest tolerance that still covers likely price movement before confirmation.

item.title: How to Top Up a Derivatives Account on a New Network
item.description: To top up a derivatives account on an unfamiliar network, check what deposits it accepts, move the right asset to that network, then send it to your…

item.title: How to get tokens for a staking pool on another chain
item.description: Moving tokens for a staking pool means matching the accepted asset and destination chain, funding gas, and checking the route and pool rules before signing.

item.title: How to Estimate a Cross-Chain Swap Output
item.description: A cross-chain swap estimate starts with the route’s market price, then subtracts pool, protocol and transfer costs; compare net output and slippage limits before sending.

item.title: What to Check Before a Cross-Chain Swap
item.description: Check the destination network, minimum output, fees, route and refund terms before sending; each determines what arrives and what happens if execution fails.

item.title: Why Cross-Chain Token Amounts Change With Decimals
item.description: Cross-chain token amounts can change because chains store integer units with different decimal scales; swaps, fees and rounding can also change what arrives.

item.title: Check Whether a Destination Token Needs Activation
item.description: A destination can need native coin, an activated account, a token account or a memo; check the network and asset rules before sending a test amount.

item.title: What Treasury Recovery Means After a Bridge Route Fails
item.description: Bridge route failures can finalize a source transfer before delivery; recovery depends on bridge rules, treasury records and the transaction state.

item.title: Why Bridge Interfaces Show Different Token Balances
item.description: Bridge interfaces show different balances because tokens have chain-specific forms, apps refresh at different times and transfers can remain pending.
